readerTitle: When good numbers lie about product-market fit
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (재사용 운반 상자 제조사, 대형 소매업체 안의 운영팀) + 가상 적용 (치과 예약 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 숫자를 볼 때는 크기보다 원인을 본다. 할인, 강제, 일회성 수요가 사라져도 남는 숫자만 적합의 증거다.
misconception: 매출, 사용자 수, 큰 주문처럼 숫자가 오르면 제품이 시장에 맞는다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: 제품-시장 적합(product-market fit)과 고객 행동 신호에 관한 일반적인 스타트업·마케팅 개념
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 상자 제조사 계산: 연 매출 $400,000 중 한 유통사 주문 $240,000 = 60%. 2번 카드 선택지 A의 '60%'와 3번 카드 수치가 일치하는지 확인했습니다.
반값 체험 고객 40곳 중 정가 재주문 5곳(12.5%), 정가 재주문 소규모 고객 6곳은 2번 카드의 별도 신호입니다. 5곳과 6곳이 같은 집단으로 읽히지 않는지 편집 단계에서 확인하세요.
내부 도구 사례(주간 사용자 2,000명, 구 시스템 종료)와 치과 예약 앱(가입 5,000건, 20개 지점 파일럿)은 모두 가상입니다. 실제 기업이나 통계로 읽히지 않도록 illustrative 라벨을 유지합니다.

cards.title: When good numbers lie about fit
body: A crate maker just had its best year: $400,000 in orders. Across town, a team inside a big retailer launched a new scheduling tool, and 2,000 staff now use it every week.
Both teams think they've found product-market fit. Neither has. The numbers were real. What caused them wasn't the product.

image.label: Two teams celebrating in front of rising charts
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 창고에서 플라스틱 운반 상자 더미 앞에 선 작은 제조사 팀, 오른쪽은 사무실에서 노트북 앞에 선 사내 팀. 양쪽 모두 위로 치솟는 그래프를 보며 축하 중. 그래프 뒤에 희미한 그림자 손이 그래프를 밀어 올리고 있음. 실제 기업 로고 금지.

cards.title: Which signal would you trust most?
body: You make reusable plastic crates for food distributors. In your first year, you collected these signals.
Which one best shows that customers truly want your crates?

options.text: A national distributor placed one order worth 60% of your yearly sales
options.feedback: It's big and it's real money. But one buyer may be testing, filling a gap or doing a favor. It tells you about one customer, not a market.

options.text: Six small customers reordered at full price without a sales call
options.feedback: The number is small, but nothing pushed them. They came back because the crates did a job, and that's the hardest signal to fake.

options.text: Over 300 trade show visitors asked for a price sheet
options.feedback: Interest is a start, but asking for a price costs nothing. You gain a list of leads, but you don't learn who will pay.

cards.title: The big year came from pushes, not pull.
body: Look closer at the $400,000. One distributor ordered $240,000 to cover a shortage from its usual supplier. It hasn't ordered since.
Another 40 customers tried the crates at half price during a launch deal. Only five reordered once the price went back up.
Take away the shortage and the discount, and the real demand is a few small, loyal buyers. That's a starting point, not fit.

cards.eyebrow: Business two · A team inside a company
cards.title: 2,000 users, because there was no other option.
body: A retailer's operations team built a tool for planning staff shifts. Usage jumped to 2,000 people a week, and leadership called it a success.

But the old system had been switched off, so staff had to log in. When the team visited stores, many managers still planned shifts in their own spreadsheets and copied the result into the tool at the end.
Usage was high. Want was low.

image.label: Store manager with the official tool open beside a personal spreadsheet
image.brief: 매장 뒷방 책상. 노트북 화면에는 회사 공식 근무표 도구가 열려 있지만 거의 비어 있고, 옆 화면이나 종이에는 직접 만든 스프레드시트가 빼곡함. 매니저는 스프레드시트를 보며 공식 도구로 옮겨 적는 중. 실제 소프트웨어 로고 금지.

cards.title: False signs of fit
body: **False signs of fit** are numbers that look like customer demand but are caused by something else, such as a mandate, a discount, a one-off need, novelty or a favor.
The test is simple. Ask: *would this number hold if the push went away?* Remove the discount, the rule or the shortage. What's left is the real signal.
Real fit is **pull**. Customers come back, pay full price and complain when you're gone.

image.label: Push arrows versus pull arrows around a product
image.brief: 가운데 상품 상자 하나. 왼쪽에서는 'Discount', 'Rule', 'Shortage', 'Favor' 라벨이 붙은 손들이 고객을 상자 쪽으로 밀고 있음. 오른쪽에서는 고객이 스스로 상자로 걸어오고, 상자에서 자석 같은 선이 고객을 끌어당김. 오른쪽에 'Pull' 라벨 강조.

cards.title: Common false signs, and the cleaner question behind each

breakdown.label: Compliments and surveys
breakdown.detail: Check: will they pay, or pay in advance?

breakdown.label: Launch or press bump
breakdown.detail: Check: who is still active two months later?

breakdown.label: A single huge customer
breakdown.detail: Check: what share of sales comes from your top buyer?

breakdown.label: Trial deals
breakdown.detail: Check: do they reorder at full price?

cards.callout: Each one is real activity. None of them proves that customers would choose you freely.

cards.title: Pushes aren't the problem. Mistaking them for pull is.
body: Every young business uses discounts, favors and a first big customer. They're useful ways to get a product into people's hands.

The mistake is counting them as proof. And a push can hide real fit too. Some required tools are genuinely loved. So ask the users, watch what they do when they have a choice, and don't throw out a good signal just because a push came with it.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app.
body: Your app helps dental clinics book appointments. After three months, you have three signals.
Which one best suggests real fit?

options.text: 5,000 signups in the week a popular newsletter featured you
options.feedback: The attention is real, but a feature brings curious visitors. Most signups from a spike never become regular users.

options.text: A large dental chain signed a paid pilot across 20 clinics
options.feedback: Money on the table counts, but a pilot is a trial, often driven by one champion. Watch whether it renews and spreads without your push.

options.text: Clinics that set up without help use it daily, and some added staff seats on their own
options.feedback: Nothing pushed these users. They chose to stay and to pay for more, which is what pull looks like.

cards.title: Before you celebrate a number, find its cause.
body: Fit is demand that stays when the discount, the rule and the favor are gone.
**Try it today:** take your best number from last month. Write down everything besides the product that could have caused it. Then find one number that none of those causes could explain.
